Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette: Kofi had always been a man who valued control and precision, traits that served him well in his long career as a software engineer. But it was a quality that made the events of 1994 all the more unbearable. As a young adult, Kofi had fled his home country as a refugee, escaping the brutal civil war that ravaged his homeland. He remembered the sound of gunfire and screams, the smell of smoke and blood, but most vividly, he recalled the faces of the soldiers who stormed into his village, their orders barked in a language he didn't understand. In the years since, Kofi had built a new life for himself in America, finding solace in the quiet routines of coding and problem-solving. But despite his outward success, the memories of that day lingered, fragmented and indistinct. Sometimes, Kofi would recall the feeling of numbness that washed over him as he watched his neighbors flee or be rounded up by the soldiers. Other times, he would see snapshots of images: a child's body lying in the dirt, a woman's face contorted in terror. But always, he felt detached, as if observing someone else's life. As Kofi grew older, these memories began to seep into his daily life. He found himself growing increasingly uneasy when given instructions or orders, whether it was from his boss or his wife. The sound of authority figures barking commands transported him back to that day in the village, and he would feel a familiar sense of disconnection wash over him. To cope, Kofi began to withdraw from social interactions, avoiding gatherings with friends and family, even skipping meetings at work. He told himself it was because he needed to focus on his coding, but deep down, he knew it was because the world outside felt too unpredictable. Kofi's attempts to manage his emotions only led to more problems. To keep his mind occupied, he would spend hours playing video games or watching TV, anything to distract him from the memories that lingered just beneath the surface. His wife, Akua, grew concerned about his increasing isolation, but Kofi reassured her that everything was fine, that he just needed some time alone. But as the months went by, Kofi's avoidance behaviors began to take a toll on his relationships and work performance. His boss expressed concerns about his missed deadlines and lack of teamwork, while Akua felt like she was losing her partner to some invisible force. Kofi knew he couldn't keep living like this, but every time he tried to reach out for help, the memories came flooding back, and he would retreat once more into his shell. It wasn't until Kofi's granddaughter asked him about his past that he realized just how much his experiences had shaped him. She was studying history in school, and her curiosity sparked something within Kofi. He began to wonder if it was time to confront the memories he had kept hidden for so long, to try to make sense of the chaos that still lingered inside him. As Kofi sat in his therapist's office, surrounded by the quiet hum of computers and the faint scent of old books, he felt a mix of trepidation and hope. What frightened him most was the possibility of losing himself completely in those memories, of becoming trapped once more in the past. But what he hoped for, more than anything, was to find some semblance of peace, to learn how to live with his experiences without being controlled by them. For the first time in decades, Kofi felt like he might be ready to face whatever lay ahead, to reclaim the life he had built and the memories that still haunted him.
